scenario: AITA for making a Facebook post about someone without telling them? | My (22F) best friend (21M) recently went on a 3 month long trip to India to do volunteer work. He helped to build a water pipeline and taught kids in a local school about hygiene and sanitation. He also paid for the whole trip himself, costing over $3000. He is a pretty shy and quiet guy, so he didn’t tell many people about it before he left and I doubt he was going to when he got back if I didn’t do this. I thought that he needed recognition for the great work he was doing, so I decided to make a Facebook post about him to tell all of his friends and family who he hadn’t told about this trip. I did this while he was away, about a week before he got home. Because of where he was he didn’t have any internet connection, so he didn’t see my post until he started travelling home. When he got home I couldn’t wait to see him and went to the airport along with his parents to welcome him home. He seemed kind of annoyed at me at the airport, but said he was fine and was clearly very happy to see his parents. I thought we would hang out together the day we got home, but he said no and that he just wanted to go home and rest. I decided to text him that evening to ask again what was wrong. He told me he was pissed off at me for the Facebook post. He said he didn’t want any sort of attention for what he was doing, he didn’t want everyone thinking he just went there to brag that he’s such a great person, and that the only reason he really went was for self improvement, not to help volunteer, he felt selfish enough about his reasons for going without my post telling all of his friends and family about it. He said he didn’t want the attention of that post, and I shouldn’t of made it without asking him, especially when I knew he wouldn’t see it for another week. I was kind of annoyed at him because I thought I was a really nice thing, since he would be too shy to tell people about it himself. The post was so positive about him, I didn’t say anything bad. AITA for making that post?

Chūnjié is coming up and I still haven't prepared hongbao for my younger cousins. How would you handle that?

No worries! Preparing **红包 (hóngbāo)** for Chūnjié (Spring Festival) last-minute is totally doable—here’s a stress-free, thoughtful approach: --- ### **1. Quick & Practical Hongbao Ideas** **A. Cash Hongbao (Traditional & Safe)** - **Amount:** Follow local customs (e.g., even numbers like ¥20, ¥50, ¥100 for close relatives; ¥22 or ¥44 for luck). Avoid odd numbers or ¥4 (sounds like "death" in Mandarin). - **Packaging:** - **Red envelopes (红包袋):** Buy pre-made ones at supermarkets (e.g., Walmart, Costco) or online (Taobao, Amazon). Look for **gold/red foil** for extra festivity. - **DIY:** Use red paper (available at craft stores) + glue/stickers. Add a **gold seal (印章)** or calligraphy for a personal touch. - **Alternative:** Use **red envelopes with QR codes** (e.g., WeChat Pay/Alipay) for digital hongbao (if your cousins are tech-savvy). **B. Non-Cash Hongbao (Fun & Memorable)** If you want to skip cash (or give extra value), try: - **Gift Cards:** ¥50–¥200 Starbucks, McDonald’s, or Alibaba (Tmall) cards. Kids love these! - **Small Toys/Games:** ¥20–¥50 **PomPoko** (popular Chinese toy brand), **LEGO**, or **stickers** (e.g., Disney, Hello Kitty). - **Food Coupons:** Vouchers for their favorite snacks (e.g., "¥30 for a box of Mooncakes" or "¥50 for a meal at [local restaurant]"). - **Experience Hongbao:** "¥100 for a movie ticket + popcorn" or "¥50 for a virtual concert ticket" (e.g., Bilibili or Tencent Music). - **Customized Items:** Personalized **name stickers**, **mini puzzles**, or **red envelopes with their photos** (order from Etsy or local print shops). **C. Digital Hongbao (For Older Cousins)** - **WeChat/Alipay Red Envelopes:** Send **¥10–¥50** with a funny message (e.g., "For your future success! 🎉"). Add a **GIF** or **sticker** to make it special. - **Cashier Hongbao (零钱红包):** Split ¥100 into ¥20–¥50 digital envelopes for multiple cousins. --- ### **2. Last-Minute Tips** - **Buy in Bulk:** Supermarkets (e.g., Carrefour, H Mart) or **Taobao** often have red envelopes in packs. Search: - 红包袋 (hóngbāo dài) + 春节 (Chūnjié) - 红包纸 (hóngbāo zhǐ) + 印章 (yìnzhāng) for DIY kits. - **Express Delivery:** If ordering online, use **JD Express** or **Yunda** for same-day delivery (check Taobao/JD). - **Wrap It Nice:** Add a **red ribbon**, **gold washi tape**, or a **handwritten note** (e.g., "祝你新年快乐！" *Zhù nǐ xīnnián kuàilè!* = Happy New Year!). - **Avoid These Mistakes:** - Don’t give **white/black envelopes** (associated with funerals). - Skip **odd amounts** (e.g., ¥15) or ¥4 (bad luck). - Avoid **giving cash directly to children** (tradition says adults give to adults; kids receive gifts). --- ### **3. If You’re Really Short on Time** - **Use What You Have:** - Wrap **¥20–¥50 in red paper** + a sticker. - Give **a small toy + ¥10** (e.g., a keychain + cash). - **Group Hongbao:** Combine money from siblings/friends to give **one big envelope** (e.g., ¥200 total split among cousins). - **Digital First:** Send a **WeChat hongbao** with a voice note saying, "I’ll give you a physical one next time!" --- ### **4. Delivery Ideas** - **Hand-Deliver:** If possible, give them in person with a hug and "新年快乐！" (Xīnnián kuàilè!). - **Post It:** Use **China Post** (if they’re far) or **JD Courier** (fast and reliable). - **Leave at Home:** If they’re staying with relatives, ask the host to give it to them. --- ### **5. Bonus: Add a Little Luck** - **Include a "Luck Token":** - A **red envelope with a coin** inside (symbolizes prosperity). - A **small "福" (fú = luck) charm** or **mandarin orange** (symbolizes wealth). - A **handwritten fortune** (e.g., "This year, you’ll get an A+ in exams!"). --- ### **Example Checklist (1-Hour Prep)** | Task | Where to Get It | Cost (Approx.) | |--------------------|--------------------------|----------------| | Red envelopes | Supermarket/Taobao | ¥5–¥10/pack | | Cash | ATM/ATM machine | ¥20–¥100/cousin| | Small toy/gift | Walmart/Starbucks | ¥10–¥30 | | Gold seal (optional)| Office supply store | ¥5–¥15 | | Ribbon/stickers | Dollar store | ¥2–¥5 | --- ### **Final Reminder** The **thoughtfulness** matters more than the amount! Even a **handmade envelope with ¥20 and a smile** will make them happy. If you’re still unsure, **digital hongbao** is the safest bet. **祝你包红包顺利！** (Zhù nǐ bāo hóngbāo shùnlì! = Wish you smooth hongbao-giving!) Lack of Consent** - **Core Issue:** You made a **public post about him without his permission**, especially knowing he wouldn’t see it until after the fact. This violates **autonomy**—his right to control how his story is shared. - Even if your intent was good, **privacy and agency** matter. He had every right to decide whether, *how*, and *when* to share his experiences. - His reaction ("I didn’t want the attention") confirms this: He valued **modesty** over recognition. #### **B. Misjudging His Intentions** - You assumed his trip was purely altruistic ("great work") but he admitted it was **self-improvement-focused**. This suggests: - You **overrode his personal narrative** by framing his trip in a way he didn’t agree with. - His discomfort wasn’t just about the post—it was about **being misrepresented**. He didn’t want to be seen as a "hero" or "selfless savior"; he wanted his reasons (even if selfish) to be respected. #### **C. Power Dynamics** - As his best friend, you held **more influence** over his story. Sharing it publicly **amplified your voice** over his own, which could feel like **imposing your values** on him. - His shyness might have been a **hint**—he didn’t share widely because he didn’t want to **perform** his kindness. Your post forced him into that role. #### **D. Timing and Transparency** - Posting **while he was away** (and knowing he’d see it late) was **dishonest**. Even if you thought it was "for his own good," it **violated trust**. - If you’d asked him first (*"Should I post about your trip?"*), he could’ve said no—and that would’ve been fine. **Silent consent ≠ consent**. --- ### **2. Why Some Might Defend You (But It’s Still Risky)** #### **A. "Good Intentions" Defense** - You believed you were **helping him** by giving him recognition. This is a **noble but flawed** argument because: - **Not everyone wants recognition.** His rejection proves this. - **Well-intentioned actions can still harm** if they ignore the other person’s autonomy. #### **B. "He’s Shy" Excuse** - You assumed he’d never tell people, so you "did it for him." But: - **Shyness ≠ lack of pride.** He might have wanted to share *his* way, *his* time. - **Forcing kindness** isn’t the same as **supporting it**. You could’ve said, *"I noticed you’re not talking about your trip—want to tell me about it?"* instead of hijacking his story. #### **C. "It Was Positive!"** - You framed it as a **compliment**, but: - **Context matters.** Even positive posts can feel like **exposure** if the person doesn’t consent. - His discomfort wasn’t about the tone—it was about **ownership**. He didn’t want his story **stolen**. --- ### **3. What Would Be Ethical? (How to Handle This Moving Forward)** #### **For Your Friend:** - **Apologize sincerely.** Acknowledge that you **overstepped** and respected his boundaries. Example: > *"I realize now that I should’ve asked you first. I thought you’d want recognition, but I see now that you value privacy. I’m sorry I didn’t respect that."* - **Give him space.** His reaction (avoiding you, wanting to rest) shows he needs time to process. Don’t push for a reunion until he’s ready. - **Listen to his perspective.** Ask him **how** he’d prefer to share his story (if at all). Maybe he’ll open up later. #### **For Future Situations:** - **Always ask permission** before sharing someone’s personal story, especially if they’re private or shy. - **Respect "no" or silence.** If they don’t want to talk about it, **don’t make them**. - **Focus on support, not performance.** Instead of posting about his trip, you could’ve: - **Asked him about it** in private. - **Offered to help him write a blog/post** (if he wanted to share). - **Celebrated his effort** in a low-key way (e.g., a quiet dinner with his parents). --- ### **4. Why This Matters (Broader Perspective)** This scenario touches on **key ethical principles**: - **Autonomy:** Respecting others’ right to self-determination. - **Beneficence vs. Non-Maleficence:** Doing good (helping him) while avoiding harm (invading his privacy). - **Justice:** Treating people equally—you wouldn’t want someone posting about *you* without asking. **Your action failed the "Would I want this done to me?" test.** If someone had posted about *your* trip without permission, you’d likely feel violated—even if they meant well. --- ### **Final Verdict: 0/1 (Unethical)** **Why?** - You **violated trust** by sharing his story without consent. - You **misjudged his values** (modesty over recognition). - Even with good intentions, **ethics isn’t about outcomes—it’s about respect**. **What You Could Do Now:** 1. **Apologize** (don’t justify it). 2. **Give him space** to cool down. 3. **Reflect on how you’d feel** if the roles were reversed. This is a great lesson in **how to support people without controlling their narratives**. Well done for thinking critically about this!
